assessments.reasoning: The publisher-governing acquisition came from GNU's fdl-1.1.txt. Its four controlled ranges locate the opening permission, the §1 definition, the §2 conditions and the Addendum. The opening directly establishes the claimed permission. The other passages resolve the apparent tension between an unalterable license document and a work-specific notice. Section 10 was visible in the same complete body as context.

challenge.method: Tested the opening permission against an unchanged official plaintext, an instrument edited to remove later-version wording from its Addendum, and the SPDX-generated license text. Compared the Addendum with a hypothetical work notice selecting 1.1 only, then checked §10 against a distinct grant expressly allowing later versions.
challenge.results: The unchanged plaintext meets the verbatim condition. Editing the Addendum changes the instrument even if the edit would make its example resemble the work's notice. The SPDX text also differs concretely: its copyright block uses a Boston street address where the pinned GNU plaintext gives the FSF website. For the hypothetical 1.1-only work, preserve its actual notice separately and leave the publisher's Addendum intact. Its sample later-version language does not enlarge the work's grant. Under §10, an actual notice expressly allowing later versions gives a choice of the specified version or a later, published, non-draft FSF version.

limitations: Revision 1 covers the complete 18,101-byte GNU plaintext identified by SHA-256 1040f0fffcf5a73398512aaa3f7cf89b7e4bb8feb13c661ad71184e015c7fcb6.
The work's actual authorized notice supplies its edition choice and feature designations. The cases here are hypothetical.
reasoning: The opening of the FSF plaintext grants everyone permission to copy and distribute the license document verbatim and expressly excludes changes. Section 1 defines the covered Document through a notice placed by its copyright holder. Section 2 governs copying that work. It requires every copy to carry the license, copyright notices and the notice applying the license. It also bars added conditions and technical restrictions on reading or further copying. The Addendum illustrates how a work can carry both the license and its own notice.
